mainTopic: מודה בקנס ואחר כך באו עדים: when a thief's admission exempts him from the fine, and the מחלוקת of סומכוס and the רבנן
overview: This amud asks whether a thief who admits to an act that carries a fine is freed from that fine, even if witnesses come afterward. First the גמרא reads the משנה closely. An admission that adds no payment of קרן counts only like 'one witness,' but a real admission that makes him owe the קרן exempts him from the fine. Next it brings a ברייתא about a thief who saw witnesses coming and admitted the theft. It tries to prove from its wording that admitting to slaughter is not a real הודאה. That proof is pushed off, because the fine of four or five is one unit, and once the כפל part falls away, the whole fine falls away. Then the גמרא asks whether this question is a מחלוקת between the רבנן and סומכוס in another ברייתא about witnesses proven to be זוממין. One explanation says they argue about whether admitting to slaughter counts. רב אחא בריה דרב איקא says instead that they argue about testimony that cannot be made זוממין, and the גמרא limits the usual rule against such testimony. Finally the גמרא asks why the false witnesses should pay a full כפל, and רבי אלעזר in the name of רב begins to correct the wording of the ברייתא; the corrected wording continues on the next amud.

steps.title: What the משנה's detailed case is really teaching
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the משנה chose the case of theft proven by two witnesses on purpose. In that case, the thief's admission to slaughtering does not make him pay any קרן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't the משנה teaching us this: he stole based on two witnesses, and slaughtered based on one witness or based on his own admission. In that case his admission does not obligate him in the קרן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers why the משנה described the theft as proven by two witnesses. That detail tells us his admission to the slaughter did not obligate him to pay the קרן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The theft was already proven by two witnesses, so the קרן is owed anyway. His admission adds nothing he has to pay. So it is not a 'real' הודאה that would exempt him from a fine.

keyTerms.term: אֶלָּא לָאו הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
keyTerms.meaning: Rather, isn't this what it is teaching us
Based on his own admission
The principal: the basic value of what was stolen
Based on two witnesses

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לָאו הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן:
phrases.english: Rather, is it not that this is what it teaches us:
He stole based on two witnesses
and slaughtered based on one witness
or based on his own admission
it is where he does not obligate himself in the principal,
phrases.notes: The theft was already proven by two witnesses, so his words don't add any new payment.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָאו הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the earlier question of why the משנה specified a theft proven by two witnesses.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The detail shows a case where the admission does not obligate the thief in the קרן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does the משנה describe such a detailed case?

steps.title: Only here is an admission treated like one witness
steps.stepSummary: Only in this kind of case is an admission treated like a single witness. Just as a second witness can join a first one and make the thief liable, witnesses who come after the admission make him liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Only in that case do we say his own admission is like one witness. With one witness, when another witness comes and joins him, the thief becomes liable. So too with his own admission: when witnesses come, he becomes liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the comparison in the משנה between 'his own admission' and 'one witness.' It says this comparison works only when the admission did not obligate him in the קרן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One witness alone cannot make a thief pay, but a second witness can join him and make him liable. An admission that obligated him in nothing is just as weak. So later witnesses make him liable for the fine, and the admission does not protect him.

keyTerms.meaning: Similar to, like
A single witness, which alone is not enough to make someone pay
Joins together, combines to make a full testimony
He becomes liable

phrases.english: that is where we say

phrases.aramaic: עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ דּוּמְיָא דְּעַל פִּי עֵד אֶחָד;
phrases.english: his own admission is similar to one witness;
just as with one witness:
when another witness comes
he joins together with him, and he becomes liable;
with his own admission too:
when witnesses come, he becomes liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא דְּאָמְרִינַן עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ דּוּמְיָא דְּעַל פִּי עֵד אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the meaning of the reading given in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An admission that does not obligate the קרן is like one witness, and later witnesses make the thief liable for the fine.

steps.title: When the admission does obligate the principal, it exempts him from the fine
steps.stepSummary: If the theft itself rests only on one witness or on his own admission, his admission obligates him in the קרן. Then it is not compared to one witness.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he stole, slaughtered and sold, all based on one witness or his own admission, he obligates himself in the קרן. Then we do not say his admission is like one witness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the contrast that finishes the proof. A real admission, one that makes him pay the קרן, is not treated like a weak single witness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here nothing else proves the theft, so his words alone make him owe the קרן. That makes it a true הודאה. The rule of מודה בקנס פטור then applies, and later witnesses do not make him pay the fine.

keyTerms.meaning: But, introducing the contrasting case
We do not say
One who admits to an act that carries a fine; he is exempt from the fine

steps.whatToRemember: An admission exempts from a fine only when it is a real הודאה, meaning it made the thief pay something (the קרן). If two witnesses already proved the theft, his admission to slaughtering counts only as 'one witness,' and later witnesses make him liable.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the משנה says admissions never exempt from a fine. The comparison to one witness applies only when the admission added no payment of קרן.

phrases.english: But if he stole, slaughtered and sold

phrases.aramaic: עַל פִּי עֵד אֶחָד אוֹ עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ –
phrases.english: based on one witness or based on his own admission,
where he obligates himself in the principal,
we do not say

phrases.aramaic: עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ דֻּומְיָא דְּעַל פִּי עֵד אֶחָד.
phrases.english: that his own admission is similar to one witness.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל גָּנַב וְטָבַח וּמָכַר עַל פִּי עֵד אֶחָד אוֹ עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite case, which completes the proof from the משנה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A real admission that obligates the קרן exempts the thief from the fine even if witnesses come later, so the משנה supports this view.

steps.title: The supporting ברייתא: a thief who admits as witnesses approach
steps.stepSummary: The second source is a ברייתא: a thief saw witnesses coming and admitted to stealing but denied slaughtering or selling. He pays only the קרן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא, as it is taught: If he saw witnesses approaching and said, 'I stole, but I did not slaughter and did not sell,' he pays only the קרן.
steps.whatsHappening: After the משנה, the גמרא now brings the ברייתא as a second source of support.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The thief admitted the theft before the witnesses testified. The ברייתא rules he pays only the קרן, with no כפל. That suggests his admission exempts him from the fine even though witnesses then came.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה
Approaching, on their way
He pays only

phrases.english: The baraita: as it is taught:
If he saw witnesses who were approaching,
and said: "I stole,
but I did not slaughter and I did not sell"
he pays only the principal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from the משנה, the גמרא brings a second source.
steps.raayaObject: That a thief who admits to an act carrying a fine is exempt from the fine even if witnesses then come.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a thief who admitted as witnesses were approaching and pays only the קרן.

steps.title: Why does the ברייתא use such complicated wording?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא has the thief say 'I stole but did not slaughter or sell.' It could have used a simpler wording.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why does it need to teach, 'and he said: I stole, but I did not slaughter and did not sell'? Let it teach, 'either I stole, or I slaughtered and sold'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the exact wording of the ברייתא. This sets up the next move, where the wording will be used to prove the point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא only wanted to teach that admitting a theft exempts him from כפל, a simple 'I stole' would be enough. The extra words 'but I did not slaughter or sell' must teach something more. The גמרא will explain what in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it to teach
Let it teach
I slaughtered
I sold

phrases.english: Why do I need it to teach:
"and he said: I stole
but I did not slaughter and I did not sell"?
Let it teach: "Either I stole
or I slaughtered and sold"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks closely at the wording of the ברייתא just quoted, to get the proof out of it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the ברייתא's longer wording teach that a simpler wording would not?

steps.title: The hidden lesson: admitting to slaughter does not count
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא chose its wording to show a contrast. A thief who admits the theft is exempt. But a thief who denied the theft and only admitted the slaughter is liable once witnesses come. So admitting to slaughter is not a real admission.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what the ברייתא teaches: he is exempt only because he said 'I stole,' which made him obligate himself in the קרן. But if he said 'I did not steal,' witnesses came and proved he stole, and then he said 'I slaughtered and sold,' and witnesses came and proved he slaughtered and sold, he did not obligate himself in the קרן, so he is liable. This shows that admitting to slaughter is not considered an admission.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 5 about the ברייתא's wording. It uses that answer as proof that admitting to slaughter is not a real admission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption comes from admitting the theft itself, because that admission makes him owe the קרן. Admitting only to the slaughter does not make him owe anything new, so it does not count. That is why later witnesses can still make him pay four or five.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, this is what it teaches us
Admission (a person admitting something against himself)
Slaughtering (of the stolen animal)
Apparently, this shows that

phrases.english: Rather, this is what it teaches us:
The reason is that he said, "I stole"
which made him obligate himself in the principal; that is why he is exempt.
But if he said, "I did not steal"
and witnesses came and said that he stole,
and then he went back and said, "I slaughtered, I sold"
and witnesses came and said that he slaughtered or sold it,
since he did not obligate himself in the principal, he is liable.
phrases.notes: Liable here means he pays the full fourfold or fivefold payment.

phrases.aramaic: אַלְמָא הוֹדָאָה דִּטְבִיחָה לָאו הוֹדָאָה הִיא!
phrases.english: Apparently, an admission to slaughtering is not an admission!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question of step 5 and turns the answer into a proof.
steps.raayaObject: That admitting to slaughter or sale is not a legal admission.
steps.raayaSupportSource: An inference from the precise wording of the ברייתא about the thief who saw witnesses coming.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The wording 'I stole' was chosen to show that the exemption depends on admitting the theft, not the slaughter.

steps.title: No: the ברייתא teaches a different point
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The ברייתא teaches that once he admits the theft, he is exempt from four or five, even though he denied the slaughter and witnesses later proved it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: No. The ברייתא teaches this point itself: once he says 'I stole,' even though he said 'I did not slaughter or sell,' and witnesses came and proved he slaughtered and sold, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from step 6. It gives a different reason the ברייתא used that wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's lesson is not about whether admitting to slaughter counts. It shows how strong the admission of theft is: it exempts him even from the fourfold or fivefold payment that the slaughter witnesses would otherwise bring. So nothing can be learned about an admission of slaughter.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches us this very point itself
Exempt

phrases.english: They say: No,
it is teaching us this very thing:
that once he said, "I stole,"

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּאָמַר ״לֹא טָבַחְתִּי וְלֹא מָכַרְתִּי״,
phrases.english: even though he said, "I did not slaughter and I did not sell,"
and witnesses came and said that he slaughtered or sold it, he is exempt.
phrases.notes: Exempt from the fourfold or fivefold payment. He still pays the קרן he admitted to.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: לָא, הִיא גּוּפַהּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof drawn in step 6.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the ברייתא's wording.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The wording can be explained another way: it shows the admission of theft exempts him even when the slaughter is proven by witnesses.

steps.title: Why is he exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why admitting the theft should exempt him from the fine for slaughtering, when witnesses proved the slaughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up the next move by asking for the reason behind the exemption in step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is surprising: the slaughter was proven by real witnesses, and he never admitted it. So why should his admission to the theft cancel the fine for the slaughter?

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source or reason behind the ruling in step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why admitting the theft exempts him from the fine for slaughter that was proven by witnesses.

steps.title: The fine is one package: four or five, never three or four
steps.stepSummary: The תורה set a fine of four or five as one whole unit. Once he is exempt from the כפל part by admitting, what would be left is only three or four, and the תורה never set a fine like that.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תורה spoke of a payment of four and five, not a payment of four for an ox or three for a sheep.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question of step 8 using the Torah's wording about the thief's payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fourfold or fivefold payment includes the קרן and the כפל inside it. If admitting the theft removes the כפל, only a threefold payment (sheep) or fourfold payment (ox) would remain. Since the תורה never set such a fine, he pays no fine at all.

keyTerms.meaning: The fourfold (sheep) and fivefold (ox) payment for slaughtering or selling a stolen animal
The Merciful One (the Torah)
The double payment a thief pays

steps.whatToRemember: Admitting the theft takes away the כפל. The four or five payment depends on the כפל, so it falls away too. It is all or nothing.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why one admission can cancel a fine for a different act that was proven by witnesses.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think of four or five as a separate fine added on top of the כפל. It is one unit that already includes the קרן and the כפל.

phrases.english: The Merciful One said a payment of four or five,
phrases.notes: שמות 21:37. The word in round brackets is in the printed גמרא, but some versions leave it out.

phrases.english: and not a payment of four (for an ox)
and not a payment of three (for a sheep).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The Torah's fine is a whole unit of four or five. A partial fine of three or four does not exist.

steps.title: Maybe this is an argument between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the question may be a מחלוקת between תנאים. It begins quoting a ברייתא: two witnesses testified to a theft and two to a slaughter, and the theft witnesses were found to be עדים זוממין. The first opinion says testimony that is partly cancelled is cancelled entirely.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say it is like a dispute of תנאים: two witnesses testified that he stole, and two testified that he slaughtered or sold. The theft witnesses were proven זוממין. Testimony that is partly cancelled is entirely cancelled.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new move. It suggests the issue may be argued by תנאים and starts quoting a ברייתא to show that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the theft testimony falls, the slaughter testimony falls with it, because the slaughter only matters if there was a theft. The גמרא is preparing to compare this with a second opinion in the ברייתא, which continues past this point.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say it is like an argument between תנאים
They were proven to be עדים זוממין (lying witnesses who could not have been there)
Testimony that is partly cancelled is entirely cancelled

phrases.english: Let us say it is like a dispute between תנאים:
two were testifying that he stole,

phrases.aramaic: וְהָיוּ שְׁנַיִם מְעִידִים אוֹתוֹ שֶׁטָּבַח וּמָכַר;
phrases.english: and two were testifying about him that he slaughtered or sold;
the theft witnesses were proven to be lying witnesses,
testimony that was partly cancelled is entirely cancelled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from explaining the ברייתא to asking whether תנאים argue about this issue.
steps.raayaObject: That the opinion under discussion depends on an argument between תנאים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about theft witnesses who were proven זוממין while the slaughter witnesses were not.

steps.title: The second case: the slaughter witnesses are proven false
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's first opinion rules on the case where the slaughter witnesses become עדים זוממין. The thief pays כפל, and the false witnesses pay three.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the witnesses about the slaughter were proven to be עדים זוממין, the thief pays double, and the false witnesses pay three.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues from step 10. Now it is the slaughter witnesses, not the theft witnesses, who are proven to be lying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The theft testimony is still good, so the thief owes the כפל for stealing. The slaughter witnesses tried to add the extra fine on top of that. So they must pay that extra amount themselves.

keyTerms.meaning: The witnesses who testified about the slaughter
They were proven to be עדים זוממין (witnesses who were somewhere else)
Double payment, the fine for a thief

phrases.english: If the witnesses of the slaughter were proven to be conspiring witnesses –
he pays the double payment,
and they pay a payment of three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the first opinion in the ברייתא that step 10 began quoting.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When only the slaughter witnesses are הוזמו, the thief pays כפל and the false witnesses pay the extra three.

steps.title: סומכוס's different ruling
steps.stepSummary: In the name of סומכוס, they said the witnesses pay the כפל and the thief pays three for an ox and two for a ram.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said in the name of סומכוס: the witnesses pay the double payment, and the thief pays three for an ox and two for a ram.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a second opinion, from סומכוס. He flips who pays which part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For סומכוס, the witnesses pay the כפל and the thief pays the rest of the full fine. Five minus two leaves three for an ox. Four minus two leaves two for a sheep. The ברייתא does not say which case he means; the גמרא works that out in steps 13-16.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox (its full fine is five)
A ram (its full fine is four)

phrases.english: They said in the name of Sumakhos:
they (the witnesses) pay the double payment,
and he (the thief) pays a payment of three for an ox
phrases.notes: The full fine for an ox is five. Two is taken off for the כפל, so three is left.

phrases.english: and two for a ram.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives סומכוס's opposing view inside the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The witnesses pay the כפל, and the thief pays the remainder: three for an ox and two for a sheep.

steps.title: Which case is סומכוס talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which part of the ברייתא סומכוס is arguing about.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which case is סומכוס referring to?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple question: which of the two cases is סומכוס arguing about? It is setting up a test of each option.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא had two cases: the theft witnesses proven false (step 10) and the slaughter witnesses proven false (step 11). סומכוס's words don't say which one he means.

keyTerms.meaning: On which one is he standing? (Which case does he mean?)

phrases.english: To which (case) is Sumakhos referring?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks where סומכוס's statement fits in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether סומכוס is arguing on the first case or the second case.

steps.title: He can't mean the first case
steps.stepSummary: If סומכוס meant the first case, where the theft witnesses were proven false, that would mean he rejects the rule that partly cancelled testimony is fully cancelled.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say he means the first case: does סומכוס not hold that testimony that is partly cancelled is entirely cancelled?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the first option and pushes it away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case the theft testimony fell apart. By the rule from step 10, the whole testimony falls with it, so the thief would owe nothing. The גמרא assumes סומכוס also holds this rule, so his ruling that the thief pays three or two cannot fit here.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say
The first part of the source
Testimony that is partly cancelled is entirely cancelled

phrases.english: If you say (he refers) to the first clause –
phrases.notes: The first clause is the case in step 10, where the theft witnesses were proven false.

phrases.english: does Sumakhos not hold
testimony that is partly cancelled is entirely cancelled?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests and rejects the first possible answer to step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading סומכוס as arguing on the first case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the theft testimony is cancelled, everything falls, so the thief can't owe three or two.

steps.title: He can't mean the second case either
steps.stepSummary: If סומכוס meant the second case, the חכמים's ruling is simply correct, so what would he argue about?
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he means the last case, the חכמים are saying it well: the thief pays double, and they (the witnesses) pay three!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the second option and pushes it away too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the second case, the theft was proven by good witnesses, so the thief really owes the כפל. Only the slaughter witnesses lied, so they should pay what they tried to add. The חכמים's ruling makes perfect sense, so it is hard to see why סומכוס would argue.

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of the source
They are saying it well (their view is reasonable)
The חכמים, here the first opinion in the ברייתא

phrases.english: But rather (he refers) to the last clause –
phrases.notes: The last clause is the case in step 11, where the slaughter witnesses were proven false.

phrases.english: the Rabbis are saying it well:
he pays the double payment,
and they pay a payment of three!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the second and last possible answer to step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading סומכוס as arguing on the second case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חכמים's ruling in this case is plainly logical, so there is nothing for סומכוס to dispute.

steps.title: סומכוס is talking about a different case
steps.stepSummary: The disagreement is about another case. The thief admitted stealing, slaughtering and selling, but denied that the first witnesses saw him. He proved them false. Then the owner brought new witnesses who proved the theft and slaughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, they argue about a different case. Two witnesses came and said to him, "You stole." He said to them, "Yes, I stole and slaughtered and sold, but I did not steal in front of you." He brought witnesses who proved them to be עדים זוממין, so he did not steal in front of them. Then the owner brought witnesses who testified that he stole, slaughtered and sold.
steps.whatsHappening: Since neither case in the ברייתא fits, the גמרא describes a new case where סומכוס and the חכמים disagree. This step only sets up the case; what each side holds comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Several things happen in order. First the thief admits the theft and the slaughter. Then the first witnesses are proven false. Last, real witnesses prove the theft and the slaughter. This mix of an admission, false witnesses and later true witnesses is what creates the question of who pays which part.

keyTerms.meaning: A different matter
There is (a difference) between them
Not in front of you
The owner of the animal

steps.confusionAlert: The thief is not denying the theft. He admits he stole, slaughtered and sold. He only denies that these witnesses saw it.

phrases.english: Rather, there is a different matter between them –
for example, where two came
and said to him, "You stole";
he said to them: "Yes, I stole,
and I slaughtered and I sold,
but I did not steal in front of you,"
and he brought witnesses and proved them to be conspiring witnesses –
that he did not steal in front of them;
and the owner brought witnesses
and they testified against him
that he stole and slaughtered and sold.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the problem of steps 14 and 15 by moving סומכוס's dispute to a new case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the dispute to a different case (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: סומכוס must be arguing about one of the two cases written in the ברייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is arguing about a case with an admission, false first witnesses, and later true witnesses.

steps.title: They argue about the admission to slaughtering
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא names the exact point of the dispute: whether the thief's admission to slaughtering counts as an admission.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they argue about the admission of slaughtering.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer by naming the exact issue that סומכוס and the רבנן argue about. This line sets up the next two steps, which explain each side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the case from step 16, the thief admitted to stealing, slaughtering and selling. The question is not about the theft. It is whether his words about the slaughter count as a real הודאה that exempts him from the extra fine.

keyTerms.meaning: An admission; when someone admits on his own to a fine (קנס), he is exempt from it
Slaughtering the stolen animal, which leads to the four-or-five payment
They argue

phrases.english: And they argue about the admission of slaughtering –
phrases.notes: "They" means סומכוס and the רבנן, about the case the גמרא just described.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer from step 16 by naming the issue in that case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It looked as if סומכוס must either reject the rule that testimony partly cancelled is entirely cancelled, or have nothing to argue about.
steps.terutzMaskana: He argues about whether the slaughter admission counts, in a case where the theft admission was forced by witnesses.

steps.title: The רבנן: the slaughter admission still counts
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן hold that even though he admitted the theft only because of the witnesses, his admission to the slaughter is a real admission, so he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן hold: even though he admitted the theft only because of the witnesses, his admission to the slaughter is a real admission, and he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the view of the רבנן. They say the thief's admission to slaughtering counts, so he does not pay the extra four-or-five fine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Admitting to something only because witnesses already testified does not count as admitting on your own. The רבנן say this is true only for the theft part. The slaughter part still counts as his own admission, so it exempts him from the slaughter fine.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages, who disagree with סומכוס here
Because of the witnesses, meaning forced by their testimony and not freely given
Exempt

phrases.english: For the Rabbis hold:
even though the admission of the theft
he admits it only because of the witnesses,
phrases.notes: These are the first witnesses, the ones he later proved false.

phrases.english: the admission of the slaughter is an admission,
and he is exempt.
phrases.notes: Exempt from the extra fine for slaughtering. He still pays the double payment for the theft.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first side of the dispute named in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The admission to slaughtering counts even when the theft admission was forced by witnesses, so the thief is exempt from the four-or-five payment.

steps.title: סומכוס: the slaughter admission does not count
steps.stepSummary: סומכוס holds that since the theft admission was only because of the witnesses, the slaughter admission does not count either.
steps.simpleTranslation: סומכוס holds: since he admitted the theft only because of the witnesses, his admission to the slaughter is not an admission.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains סומכוס's side. For him, the slaughter admission goes together with the forced theft admission, so neither one counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The slaughter fine only matters if there was a theft. Since he admitted the theft only because of the witnesses, סומכוס says his words about the slaughter do not count as admitting on his own. So nothing exempts him from the slaughter fine.

keyTerms.meaning: Since, because
Is not an admission

phrases.english: And Sumakhos holds:
since the admission of the theft
he admits it only because of the witnesses,
the admission of the slaughter is not an admission.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing side to the רבנן in step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the theft admission was forced by witnesses, the slaughter admission does not count as an admission.

steps.title: So the false witnesses pay double and the thief pays the extra fine
steps.stepSummary: According to סומכוס, the first witnesses, who were proven false, pay כפל, and the thief pays three more for an ox and two more for a ram.
steps.simpleTranslation: And those first witnesses, whom he proved false, pay the double payment, and he pays three for an ox and two for a ram.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how סומכוס's opinion leads to the words he said in step 12. Now his statement fits the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first witnesses were proven false, so they pay the כפל they tried to make him pay. The new witnesses proved the theft and the slaughter, and his admission does not exempt him. So the thief pays the full fine: three more for an ox and two more for a ram.

keyTerms.meaning: He proved them to be עדים זוממין, false witnesses
The double payment a thief pays
Three for an ox and two for a ram, the extra amounts beyond the double payment

steps.whatToRemember: In this first explanation, the argument is about one point. When a thief admits the theft only because of witnesses, does his admission to slaughtering still exempt him from the four-or-five payment? The רבנן say yes. סומכוס says no, so the thief pays the extra amounts, and the false witnesses pay כפל. The next step (רב אחא) rejects this explanation.
steps.confusionAlert: Two different payments go to two different people here. The false witnesses pay כפל to the thief, because that is what they tried to make him pay. The thief pays the fine to the owner, based on the new witnesses.

phrases.english: And those first witnesses whom he proved false –
pay the double payment;
and he pays
three for an ox and two for a ram.
phrases.notes: These come on top of the double payment, making five for an ox and four for a sheep.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses סומכוס's view from step 19 to explain his statement in step 12.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: סומכוס's statement fits the case where the theft admission was forced by witnesses. The false witnesses pay כפל, and the thief pays the full four-or-five payment because his slaughter admission does not count.

steps.title: רב אחא rejects the idea that the dispute is about admitting to slaughter
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא says no. Everyone agrees that admitting to slaughter is not a real admission.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא said: No. Everyone agrees that admitting to slaughtering is not a real admission.
steps.whatsHappening: A new אמורא pushes back on the explanation from the last few steps. He says the רבנן and סומכוס do not argue about whether admitting to slaughter counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 17-19 put the whole dispute on one question: does admitting to slaughter count as a הודאה? רב אחא takes that question off the table, since both sides agree it does not count. So he now has to find a different point that they argue about.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees (both sides of the dispute)
An admission about slaughtering the stolen animal
It is not a real (legally binding) admission

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha son of Rav Ika said:
No; everyone agrees
an admission of slaughtering is not an admission;
phrases.notes: He means it doesn't create any payment the thief owes, so it has no legal weight.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רב אחא בריה דרב איקא לא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the explanation that the dispute is about whether admitting to slaughter counts as an admission.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The explanation of the dispute given in steps 17-19.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Both sides actually agree that admitting to slaughter is not an admission, so that cannot be what they argue about.

steps.title: The real dispute is about testimony that cannot be proven false
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא says the argument is really about עדות שאי אתה יכול להזימה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, they argue about testimony that you cannot make into זוממין testimony.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא names the new topic of the dispute. This line sets up the case he is about to describe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually, witnesses can be caught as liars through הזמה: other witnesses say 'you were with us somewhere else at that time.' רב אחא says the dispute is about witnesses who can never be caught that way. Is their testimony still valid?

keyTerms.meaning: Testimony that cannot be proven false through הזמה
Proving witnesses false by showing they were somewhere else at the time
They disagree

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא בְּעֵדוּת שֶׁאִי אַתָּה יָכוֹל לַהֲזִימָּהּ
phrases.english: Rather, about testimony that you cannot render זוממין
they disagree

steps.triggerLanguage: אלא בעדות שאי אתה יכול להזימה קמיפלגי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting the old explanation, offers a new point of dispute.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the dispute to a different legal principle.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dispute is about whether admitting to slaughter counts as an admission.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dispute is about whether testimony that cannot be made זוממין is valid.

steps.title: The case: the thief names the true witnesses himself
steps.stepSummary: The thief admits the theft but says the first witnesses weren't there and names others instead. He proves the first witnesses false. Then the people he named testify that he stole and slaughtered or sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, witnesses came and said to him, 'You stole.' He said, 'I stole, slaughtered and sold, but I didn't steal in front of you. I stole in front of so-and-so and so-and-so.' He brought witnesses and made the first ones זוממין, showing he did not steal in front of them. Then so-and-so and so-and-so came and testified that he stole, slaughtered and sold.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out the exact case where this kind of testimony comes up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key detail is that the thief himself named the later witnesses as the people who saw him steal. That means he can never prove them false. They are a clear example of עדות שאי אתה יכול להזימה.

keyTerms.meaning: Witnesses
So-and-so and so-and-so (specific people the thief names)
He made them זוממין (proved them false through הזמה)
They testified

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two sets of witnesses. The FIRST witnesses are proven false. The SECOND set, the ones the thief named, are the ones who cannot be proven false.

phrases.english: For example, where witnesses came
and said to him: 'You stole,'
and he said to them: 'I stole, and I slaughtered, and I sold,
but it was not in front of you that I stole,
rather in front of so-and-so and so-and-so';
and he brought witnesses and made them זוממין,
showing that he did not steal in their presence;
and so-and-so and so-and-so came
and testified against him that he stole and slaughtered and sold.

steps.triggerLanguage: כגון דאתו סהדי ואמרי ליה גנבת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the concrete case for the principle named in step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this case, the later witnesses were named by the thief himself, so he can never make them זוממין.

steps.title: The רבנן: testimony that can't be proven false does not count
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן hold that the later witnesses give testimony that cannot be made זוממין, and such testimony is not valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what they argue about: the רבנן hold this is testimony that you cannot make זוממין, and any testimony that you cannot make זוממין is not testimony.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the opinion of the רבנן on this case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the רבנן, testimony only counts if it could, at least in theory, be proven false through הזמה. Here the later witnesses are thrown out, so only the thief's own admission is left. He pays the principal but no fine, which is why the רבנן say he is exempt from four and five.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages (the majority opinion)
It is not valid testimony
They hold

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that, for the רבנן, being open to הזמה is part of what makes testimony valid.

phrases.english: And in this they disagree:
that the רבנן hold

phrases.aramaic: הָוְיָא לַהּ עֵדוּת שֶׁאִי אַתָּה יָכוֹל לַהֲזִימָּהּ,
phrases.english: it is testimony that you cannot render זוממין,

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל עֵדוּת שֶׁאִי אַתָּה יָכוֹל לַהֲזִימָּהּ –
phrases.english: and any testimony that you cannot render זוממין
is not testimony.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first side of the dispute in the case just described.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Testimony that cannot be made זוממין is not valid. So the later witnesses don't count, and the thief is exempt from the fine.

steps.title: סומכוס: testimony that can't be proven false still counts
steps.stepSummary: סומכוס holds that testimony that cannot be made זוממין is still valid testimony.
steps.simpleTranslation: And סומכוס holds: testimony that you cannot make זוממין is testimony.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives סומכוס's side, which explains his ruling in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For סומכוס, the later witnesses are valid, so the thief owes four or five. The first witnesses, who were proven false, pay him כפל. That is why, as step 20 said, the thief himself pays only three more for an ox and two more for a sheep.

keyTerms.meaning: It is valid testimony

steps.whatToRemember: Under רב אחא's explanation, everyone agrees that admitting to slaughter is not an admission. The real dispute is about testimony that cannot be made זוממין. The רבנן say it is not valid, so the thief is exempt. סומכוס says it is valid, so the thief pays, minus the כפל he collects from the false witnesses.

phrases.english: And סומכוס holds:
testimony that you cannot render זוממין
is testimony.

steps.triggerLanguage: וסומכוס סבר עדות שאי אתה יכול להזימה הויא עדות
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing side to the רבנן in step 24 and completes רב אחא's explanation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Testimony that cannot be made זוממין is valid. So the thief is liable, with the כפל from the false witnesses going toward his payment.

steps.title: Isn't testimony that can't be disproved invalid?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges סומכוס: we hold as a fixed rule that עדות שאי אתה יכול להזימה is not valid testimony.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we hold that testimony which cannot be made זוממין is not testimony at all!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the explanation from Step 25, where סומכוס accepts testimony that cannot be made זוממין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is an accepted rule that testimony which cannot be made זוממין does not count. It seems hard to say that סומכוס disagrees with such a basic rule. So רב אחא's way of explaining the argument looks shaky.

keyTerms.meaning: We hold as an accepted rule
Testimony that you cannot prove to be זוממין
It is not valid testimony

phrases.english: But don't we hold as an accepted rule
that testimony which you cannot make into זוממין testimony
is not testimony!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges סומכוס's position as explained in Step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אחא's claim that סומכוס accepts testimony that cannot be made זוממין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An accepted rule says such testimony is invalid, so no תנא should be described as accepting it.

steps.title: The rule only applies when witnesses can't name a time
steps.stepSummary: The rule against such testimony only applies when the witnesses do not know the day or hour. Here the thief's own admission supports the witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: That rule applies where the witnesses don't know which day or which hour, so there is no real testimony at all. But here, the thief is supporting their testimony.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by limiting the rule to one kind of case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses who cannot name a day or hour give testimony that is basically empty, so it is not valid. In our case, the thief himself admits he stole, which backs up the later witnesses. So סומכוס can accept their testimony without going against the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: These words apply (only) to
On which day, at which hour
There is no testimony at all
Support, backing up

steps.whatToRemember: The rule that testimony which cannot be made זוממין is invalid is about witnesses who give no day or hour. When the defendant's own admission supports the witnesses, סומכוס accepts them.

phrases.english: These words apply where

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא יָדְעִי בְּאֵיזֶה יוֹם בְּאֵיזֶה שָׁעָה
phrases.english: they do not know on which day, at which hour
so there is no testimony at all;
but here
it is support that is backing it up.
phrases.notes: He means the thief's own admission that he stole backs up what the later witnesses say.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule invalidates every testimony that cannot be made זוממין.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule only covers testimony with no day or hour. Testimony backed by the defendant's own admission can be valid in סומכוס's view.

steps.title: Why should the witnesses pay double?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא said the witnesses pay כפל. But the thief already admitted the theft, so he owed the קרן anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: they pay double payment. But since he admits that he stole, he has to pay the principal anyway!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the ברייתא and raises a difficulty with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The witnesses who were shown to be זוממין only tried to cause a loss that the thief did not already owe. He admitted the theft, so he owed the קרן no matter what. So it makes no sense for the witnesses to pay a full כפל, which includes that קרן.

keyTerms.meaning: Double payment
The principal, the value of what was stolen

phrases.english: The Master said:
They pay double payment.
phrases.notes: 'They' are the first witnesses, the ones the thief proved to be זוממין, according to סומכוס.

phrases.english: Since he admits that he stole,
he has to pay the principal anyway?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: הֵן מְשַׁלְּמִין תַּשְׁלוּמֵי כֶפֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the validity of the testimony to the amount the witnesses pay.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that the witnesses pay תשלומי כפל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The thief owed the קרן because of his own admission. So the witnesses could only have caused him the extra amount, not the full double.

steps.title: רב corrects the wording of the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר in the name of רב begins to change how the ברייתא should be taught.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said in the name of רב: Teach the ברייתא this way:
steps.whatsHappening: This line sets up the answer. רב is about to give a corrected wording of the ברייתא, which continues in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of explaining the ruling as it stands, רב fixes the wording of the ברייתא itself. The corrected wording will remove the problem of the witnesses paying a קרן the thief already owed.

keyTerms.meaning: In the name of רב

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rav,
Teach it this way:

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב, תְּנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the difficulty raised in Step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the wording of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא says the witnesses pay a full תשלומי כפל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא should be read with different wording, which is given in the next part of the text.
